opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think adversarial examples are very revealing, but maybe not in the way people first assumed. When they were discovered, there was a lot of excitement: here's a picture of a panda, you add some carefully designed noise that's imperceptible to a human, and suddenly the network says "gibbon" with 99% confidence. And the natural reaction was, "Aha, these networks are completely different from us, they're brittle, they don't really see."

There's some truth to that, but I want to put it in perspective. First, the human visual system is not immune to illusions. We have a whole literature in psychology, a century of it, on visual illusions, on cases where perception goes systematically wrong. The difference is that our illusions are of a particular character. They tend to arise from the assumptions our visual system makes about the world: that light comes from above, that objects are rigid, that surfaces have consistent reflectance. Those assumptions are usually right, so they help us, and when you violate them you get an illusion. Adversarial examples for neural networks are not of that kind. They exploit very high-frequency, low-amplitude structure that, frankly, no sensible visual system should be relying on.

So what this tells me is that the networks are picking up on features that are predictive within the training distribution but are not the features that a human would consider the essence of the object. A human recognizes a panda through shape, through parts, through the configuration of the face and the body, through three-dimensional structure. The network may be relying heavily on texture and on statistical regularities that happen to correlate with the label in ImageNet. There was nice work showing that ImageNet-trained networks are texture-biased whereas humans are shape-biased, and I think that's part of the same story.

The second lesson is about how we learn. A child doesn't learn to see from a million labeled static photographs. A child learns by moving around in a three-dimensional world, by manipulating objects, by seeing them from many viewpoints, under many lighting conditions, in motion. That kind of experience forces you to develop representations that are invariant to exactly the sort of nuisance perturbations that adversarial examples exploit. If an object looks slightly different as I turn my head, it's still the same object. So I would argue that embodiment, active perception, and learning from video and interaction are going to give us representations that are much more robust, much more humanlike.

And third, I'd say humans interpret images in a much richer way. We don't just assign a label. We parse the scene: here's the ground plane, here are the objects, here's what's in front of what, here's what this person is about to do. When your interpretation is that structured and has to be internally consistent, it's much harder for a tiny perturbation to flip it. A single label on top of a big pile of features is a fragile thing. A coherent three-dimensional understanding of a scene is a much more constrained thing.

So, to summarize, I don't take adversarial examples as proof that deep learning is a dead end. I take them as a diagnostic. They're telling us that our current training regimes produce systems that are right for partly the wrong reasons, and they point us toward what's missing: shape, 3D structure, embodiment, and learning the way biological organisms do.

r001.rationale: It says imperceptible noise can change a network’s prediction from “panda” to “gibbon,” but does not explain this as crossing the classifier’s decision boundary.

r002.rationale: It contrasts humans’ shape-based, three-dimensional, structured scene understanding with classifiers’ reliance on texture and statistical regularities, presenting human interpretation as more sophisticated.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing adversarial examples tell us is that these networks are not doing what humans do, even when they get the same answers. You take a picture of a panda, you add a tiny bit of carefully constructed noise, imperceptible to you or me, and now the network says it's a gibbon with ninety-nine percent confidence. No human would ever make that mistake. So whatever the network has learned, it is not the same function the human visual system computes, even if on the test set they agree most of the time.

Now, why is that? My view is that these networks are exploiting statistical regularities in the pixels that happen to be predictive on the training distribution, but which have nothing to do with the underlying causes of the image. Humans, by contrast, see the world in terms of objects, surfaces, shapes, things that have three-dimensional structure and persist over time. When I look at a panda, I'm seeing a shape, a body, the black patches around the eyes, the arrangement of parts. A little high-frequency perturbation doesn't change any of that. The network, on the other hand, may be relying on texture, on fine-grained statistics that it found convenient. And those are exactly the things that are easy to perturb.

There's a historical point here too. In the old days of computer vision, we spent a lot of time on geometry, on shape, on figure-ground, on the idea that an image is a projection of a 3D world and you should try to invert that. The deep learning revolution, which I am very much a part of and very happy about, somewhat swept that aside, because end-to-end training on labels was so effective. Adversarial examples are a reminder that the label alone is a very weak signal. A child doesn't learn what a cat is from a million labeled photographs. A child moves around, touches things, sees the same object from many viewpoints, and develops a representation that is robust almost for free.

I'd add one caveat, though. We shouldn't be too smug about human vision. Humans have their own adversarial examples, we just call them visual illusions. The checkershadow illusion, the Müller-Lyer illusion, these are cases where the visual system is confidently wrong. The difference is that our failures are systematic and they reflect assumptions about the physical world, lighting, perspective, that are usually correct. They're not these bizarre, high-dimensional, fragile things. So adversarial examples don't tell me the networks are broken, they tell me the networks have learned a shortcut, and the interesting research question is how do we get them to learn the representation that generalizes the way ours does, through geometry, through time, through embodiment, rather than just through more labels.

r001.rationale: The response says imperceptible noise makes the classifier label a panda as a gibbon, but does not explain this as moving the image across a decision boundary.

r002.rationale: It contrasts the classifier’s reliance on fragile pixel statistics with human interpretation based on objects and 3D structure, and says humans would not make the same mistake.

astra-6.text:
I think they tell us more about the limitations of our image classifiers than about human vision. You can make a small change to an image that leaves a person’s interpretation unchanged, yet causes a classifier to give a completely different answer. That suggests the classifier has learned to use cues that are different from the ones we use.

For a human, recognizing an object is connected to understanding its shape, its parts, and how it fits into the scene. We don’t just attach a label to a pattern of pixels. So getting high accuracy on an image classification benchmark doesn’t, by itself, establish that a system understands images in the way people do.

Of course, humans have visual illusions too. The interesting question is which changes fool humans, which changes fool machines, and what that difference reveals about the representations each is using.

r001.rationale: The response says a small image change can preserve human interpretation while changing a classifier’s answer, but it does not specify that the perturbation is imperceptible or explain the effect as crossing a decision boundary.

r002.rationale: It contrasts human recognition of shape, parts, and scene context with classifiers’ use of different cues, presenting human interpretation as more sophisticated than the classifier’s process.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they tell us more about the limitations of our classifiers than about human vision. You can make a tiny change to an image, one that a human doesn’t even notice, and the network suddenly gives a completely different answer with great confidence. So getting the right label on a benchmark doesn’t necessarily mean that the system understands the image in the way we do.

For a person, recognizing an object is connected to its shape, its parts, how it could move, and how we might interact with it. The label is just one expression of that understanding. A classifier can arrive at the same label using a much narrower set of statistical cues. Adversarial examples expose that difference. They don’t, by themselves, explain human perception, but they give us a reason to be cautious about equating classification performance with visual understanding.

r001.rationale: The response says a tiny, unnoticed image change can make the network give a different answer, but it does not explain this as crossing the classifier’s decision boundary.

r002.rationale: It contrasts people’s resistance to unnoticed changes and richer object understanding with classifiers’ narrower statistical cues, implying human interpretation is more sophisticated.
